title: Solidarity Lanes: Latest figures – September 2026
source_name: 欧盟委员会交通与运输总司
content: In the face of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the EU, together with Ukraine and Moldova launched the EU-Ukraine Solidarity Lanes in May 2022, establishing new transport routes to keep Ukraine’s imports and exports flowing via rail, road and inland waterways. Today, the EU-Ukraine Solidarity Lanes have become a lifeline for Ukraine’s economy. In August 2026 the Solidarity Lanes allowed: - Nearly 100% of Ukrainian imports - Around 90% of Ukrainian exports of non-agricultural products (in comparison to around 5% through the Black Sea) - Around 90% of Ukrainian exports of grain, oilseeds and related products (in comparison to around 10% through the Black Sea) Ukrainian exports Since May 2022, the Solidarity Lanes have allowed Ukraine to export ca. 240 million tonnes (Mt) of goods, according to data from the Ukrainian customs registers. Within this amount, it can be estimated that the Solidarity Lanes enabled exports of around 108 million tonnes of Ukrainian agricultural products (including ca. 99 million tonnes of Ukrainian grain, oilseeds and related products) and around 132 million tonnes of non-agricultural goods including ores, steel and related products. In total, around 259 Mt of Ukrainian grain, oilseeds and related products were exported through the Solidarity Lanes (40%) and the Ukrainian Black Sea ports (60%) since May 2022 [1]. Imports to Ukraine The Solidarity Lanes also play a crucial role for Ukrainian imports. Since May 2022, they have allowed Ukraine to import ca. 116 Mt of goods, such as fuel, vehicles, fertilisers as well as military and humanitarian assistance. Value of trade The total value of trade via the Solidarity Lanes since May 2022 is estimated at around EUR 324 billion, with around EUR 82 billion for Ukrainian exports. The total value of imports to Ukraine is estimated at ca. EUR 241 billion. Background Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the blockade of Ukrainian seaports, Ukraine has been unable to export its produce and import what it needs via its usual transport routes. Against this background, the EU established 'Solidarity Lanes' to ensure Ukraine can export grain, iron ore, steel and other products and to import the goods it needs, from fuel to military and humanitarian assistance, via alternative transport routes: inland waterways, rail and road. The Solidarity Lanes cover trade across all sectors and are an unprecedented cooperation of authorities and businesses in EU Member States, Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova. The Solidarity Lanes’ work is carried out in close cooperation between the European Commission, concerned authorities and the transport community. The focus is on addressing bottlenecks to enhance the capacity and smooth functioning of the Solidarity Lanes to sustain Ukrainian exports and imports across sectors. This includes measures to improve traffic management and streamlining of border procedures and checks, as well as investments in infrastructure or logistics equipment. The Solidarity Lanes are also laying the ground for the longer-term connectivity between Ukraine and the EU and will play a key role for Ukraine’s reconstruction and integration in the EU single market. [1] Between May and July 2022, the Solidarity Lanes were the only option for Ukraine to export its agricultural produce. In August 2022, the UN-brokered Black Sea Grain Initiative (BSGI) helped relaunch grain shipments from Ukraine’s Black Sea ports. In mid-July 2023, Russia terminated its participation in the BSGI, which was consequently discontinued. In August 2023, Ukraine launched a new Black Sea corridor for trade vessels heading to and from Ukrainian sea ports despite Russia’s withdrawal from the BSGI. Ca. 2.4 Mt of grain, oilseeds and other related products have been exported this way in July 2026. - Publication date - 19 October 2026 - Author - Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport

title: Keynote speech by Director-General Magda Kopczyńska: The European Union’s role in ensuring a competitive European aviation in a challenging geopolitical landscape
source_name: 欧盟委员会交通与运输总司
content: *** To be checked against delivery *** Thank you for inviting me to speak at Wings of Change Europe. I don’t often get to spend time with the operational core of European aviation; it is a pleasure to do so. For years now, aviation in Europe has ridden the wave of post-deregulation growth. Passengers, airlines, airports – everyone has benefited from our leadership on the global aviation stage. But my message today is one of caution: Europe is still a world leader in aviation. But this leadership cannot be taken for granted. Today, I would like to share my views on how Europe can keep its aviation sector competitive, despite a challenging geopolitical landscape. But first, let’s remind ourselves what we’ve built. Our aviation single market has transformed connectivity across the continent. It has more than tripled direct intra-EU routes, significantly cut ticket prices, and helped air passenger numbers in the Union reach 1.1 billion by 2025. Aviation directly supports around 2 million jobs in the EU, and indirectly 9.3 million. It accounts for around 4.5% of EU GDP, and is part of a broader ecosystem supporting connectivity, trade, tourism and regional cohesion. Europe’s aerospace manufacturers ranked first for large commercial aircraft deliveries in 2025, with a 55% market share and around 60% of backlog orders. And while European technology manages 70% of global airspace, the EU is the world’s largest exporter of high-tech civil aeronautical products. But the world has changed. The world of 2026 is not that of 2015, the year of the EU Aviation Strategy. Since then, we have seen the Paris agreement, the Green Deal, the pandemic, geopolitical instability, sharper industrial rivalry, more fragile supply chains, higher energy costs, and a more fragmented global environment. In parallel, the sector is under pressure to decarbonise faster, modernise infrastructure, strengthen resilience and remain globally competitive. That is why Europe needs a new aviation strategy. Aviation is a strategic sector for Europe’s prosperity, sovereignty, innovation, connectivity and resilience. And in these volatile times, we need to be strategic. For Europe to remain an aviation leader, we need a policy framework that is broader, more industrial, more security-aware and more future-oriented. But what does this mean in practice? First, it means putting competitiveness centre stage. Preserving connectivity and affordable air services requires competitive airlines, airports, manufacturers and service providers. So we need to increase supply-chain resilience, decrease strategic dependencies, support the aeronautics industry, and ensure that the conditions for competition are fair both inside Europe, and globally. Let’s stay with this last point – fair competition – for a moment. Because I would really like to emphasise the Commission’s position on this. We are asking European operators to decarbonise, invest and innovate faster — and we stand firmly by these demands. But we also know that your sector is facing stiff competition from non-EU countries. We are determined to make sure that EU companies are never put at a permanent disadvantage compared to its competitors, which are often operating with lower costs and/or weaker constraints. Believe me, we are very focused on this. My second message today is that decarbonisation and competitiveness must go hand in hand. The Commission’s view is clear: decarbonisation is not the opposite of growth. It is the condition for aviation’s long-term growth. Sustainable aviation fuels are central to the transition, and increasing uptake is encouraging. But the challenge ahead is huge. Sustainable Aviation Fuels are still significantly more expensive than fossil kerosene, e-SAF projects face major investment barriers, and the business case for scaling up remains difficult. That is why Europe must continue to combine regulatory certainty with practical support. We need more production, more competition in fuel supply, stronger financing mechanisms, and more investment in innovation — including electric, hybrid-electric and hydrogen aircraft. This must be accompanied by work on non-CO2 impacts and cleaner operations. The objective is not only to reduce emissions, but to put Europe in the lead on the technologies, fuels and industrial capabilities of clean aviation. Third, we must address one of the clearest structural weaknesses in European aviation: air traffic management. Europe’s ATM system remains too fragmented and too dependent on outdated technologies. This affects punctuality, capacity, costs, emissions and passenger experience. In 2025 alone, ATM delays were estimated to have cost the sector more than EUR 2 billion. This is not sustainable. We need an ATM system that is more integrated, more digital and more performance-driven. That means implementing the new regulatory framework, improving network governance, accelerating technological deployment, addressing controller shortages, and moving towards interoperable, cloud-based and AI-enabled systems. A smarter, more connected European sky is not a slogan — it is an economic, environmental and strategic necessity. Fourth, we need to think of airports and infrastructure differently. Airports are no longer simple points of departure and arrival. They are becoming multimodal nodes, energy hubs, digital platforms and, increasingly, dual-use assets. They must invest in modernisation, decarbonisation, passenger experience, resilience and operational efficiency. At the same time, Europe must ensure that its regulatory framework on slots, charges and groundhandling remains fit for purpose in a more constrained and competitive environment. Infrastructure is also key for resilience and security. We have seen cyber threats, GNSS interference, drone incursions, climate-related disruptions and broader geopolitical instability in recent years. A future-proof aviation policy must include stronger cybersecurity, better crisis preparedness, more resilient fuel and data systems, and closer civil-military coordination. My fifth point is the need for more innovation — and deployment. Europe has extraordinary strengths in aeronautics, research and high-value manufacturing. But leadership requires more than new technologies. It also depends on certifying, industrialising and deploying them in Europe. And preferably before they are deployed elsewhere. So the future research and innovation agenda must be more focused and more operational: cleaner aircraft, AI-enabled ATM, sustainable aviation fuels, drones, counter-drone technologies, and dual-use capabilities. We also need strong certification capacity and a clear pathway from laboratory to market. Scientific excellence is good. Turning that excellence into real industrial leadership is much, much better. The final part of the aviation puzzle is of course people. The sector faces workforce shortages, a wave of retirements and changing skills needs. To succeed in the green and digital future, aviation must remain attractive to the next generation. We need investment in skills, training, mobility, upskilling and reskilling across the ecosystem — from engineering and manufacturing to airport operations, air traffic management and digital systems. So let me conclude. Europe starts from a position of strength. Aviation remains one of our greatest economic and strategic assets. But in a fundamentally changed context, this leadership cannot be taken for granted. The right response is not to retreat. It is to act with greater clarity, ambition and coordination. That means a strategy that supports competitiveness, preserves connectivity, accelerates decarbonisation, strengthens resilience, modernises infrastructure and turns innovation into industrial advantage. Maintaining Europe’s leadership in aviation is a shared responsibility. Industry must invest, innovate, scale and train. The EU must provide strategic direction, a stable regulatory framework, financing tools, innovation support and strong external leverage. Member States must play their part in implementation — for infrastructure, airspace, skills, security and enforcement. In today’s world we need to take care of ourselves, strengthen our autonomy, but for us that does not mean turning away from multilateralism. Europe supports ICAO because we believe joint solutions are better than fragmented ones, particularly in a global sector like aviation We support ICAO not only in words but also in our actions: we support ICAO with people and funding, including for example a large budget contributed to ACT SAF. We are also among those jurisdictions who have implemented CORSIA in law, from day 1. We will continue to support ICAO, looking forward to be in Montreal myself for the Air Transport Conference in a couple of weeks Aviation needs to adapt. But I want us to go further – I want us, here in Europe, to shape the future of aviation. And if we work together, I firmly believe that we can do that! - Publication date - 16 October 2026 - Author - Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport
